title: Beyond the Star Rating: A Scalable Framework for Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis Using LLMs and Text Classification
summary: Customer-provided reviews have become an important source of information for business owners and other customers alike. However, effectively analyzing millions of unstructured reviews remains challenging. While large language models (LLMs) show promise for natural language understanding, their application to large-scale review analysis has been limited by computational costs and scalability concerns. This study proposes a hybrid approach that uses LLMs for aspect identification while employing classic machine-learning methods for sentiment classification at scale. Using ChatGPT to analyze sampled restaurant reviews, we identified key aspects of dining experiences and developed sentiment classifiers using human-labeled reviews, which we subsequently applied to 4.7 million reviews collected over 17 years from a major online platform. Regression analysis reveals that our machine-labeled aspects significantly explain variance in overall restaurant ratings across different aspects of dining experiences, cuisines, and geographical regions. Our findings demonstrate that combining LLMs with traditional machine learning approaches can effectively automate aspect-based sentiment analysis of large-scale customer feedback, suggesting a practical framework for both researchers and practitioners in the hospitality industry and potentially, other service sectors.

AI.tldr: Hybrid approach combining LLMs for aspect identification and classic ML for sentiment classification enables scalable analysis of 4.7M restaurant reviews, demonstrating practical framework for large-scale customer feedback analysis.
AI.motivation: Customer reviews are valuable but challenging to analyze at scale due to unstructured nature; LLMs show promise but face computational cost and scalability limitations for large-scale review analysis.
AI.method: Hybrid approach: ChatGPT identifies key aspects from sampled restaurant reviews, then human-labeled reviews train sentiment classifiers using classic ML methods, applied to 4.7M reviews over 17 years from major platform.
AI.result: Machine-labeled aspects significantly explain variance in overall restaurant ratings across dining aspects, cuisines, and regions; hybrid approach effectively automates aspect-based sentiment analysis at scale.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLMs with traditional ML provides practical framework for large-scale customer feedback analysis in hospitality and other service sectors, balancing accuracy with computational efficiency.

title: PyVision-RL: Forging Open Agentic Vision Models via RL
summary: Reinforcement learning for agentic multimodal models often suffers from interaction collapse, where models learn to reduce tool usage and multi-turn reasoning, limiting the benefits of agentic behavior. We introduce PyVision-RL, a reinforcement learning framework for open-weight multimodal models that stabilizes training and sustains interaction. Our approach combines an oversampling-filtering-ranking rollout strategy with an accumulative tool reward to prevent collapse and encourage multi-turn tool use. Using a unified training pipeline, we develop PyVision-Image and PyVision-Video for image and video understanding. For video reasoning, PyVision-Video employs on-demand context construction, selectively sampling task-relevant frames during reasoning to significantly reduce visual token usage. Experiments show strong performance and improved efficiency, demonstrating that sustained interaction and on-demand visual processing are critical for scalable multimodal agents.

AI.tldr: PyVision-RL is a reinforcement learning framework that prevents interaction collapse in multimodal agents by using oversampling-filtering-ranking rollouts and accumulative tool rewards, enabling sustained multi-turn tool use and efficient video reasoning through on-demand context construction.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning for agentic multimodal models often suffers from interaction collapse, where models learn to reduce tool usage and multi-turn reasoning, limiting the benefits of agentic behavior. This collapse prevents models from fully leveraging their agentic capabilities.
AI.method: PyVision-RL combines an oversampling-filtering-ranking rollout strategy with an accumulative tool reward to prevent collapse and encourage multi-turn tool use. For video reasoning, PyVision-Video employs on-demand context construction, selectively sampling task-relevant frames during reasoning to reduce visual token usage. The framework uses a unified training pipeline to develop PyVision-Image and PyVision-Video for image and video understanding.
AI.result: Experiments show strong performance and improved efficiency. The framework demonstrates that sustained interaction and on-demand visual processing are critical for scalable multimodal agents, with PyVision-Video achieving significant reductions in visual token usage while maintaining strong reasoning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: PyVision-RL successfully addresses interaction collapse in multimodal agents through innovative reinforcement learning techniques. The combination of oversampling-filtering-ranking rollouts, accumulative tool rewards, and on-demand context construction enables scalable, efficient multimodal agents that maintain sustained interaction and multi-turn reasoning capabilities.

title: Prompt-Level Distillation: A Non-Parametric Alternative to Model Fine-Tuning for Efficient Reasoning
summary: Advanced reasoning typically requires Chain-of-Thought prompting, which is accurate but incurs prohibitive latency and substantial test-time inference costs. The standard alternative, fine-tuning smaller models, often sacrifices interpretability while introducing significant resource and operational overhead. To address these limitations, we introduce Prompt-Level Distillation (PLD). We extract explicit reasoning patterns from a Teacher model and organize them into a structured list of expressive instructions for the Student model's System Prompt. Evaluated on the StereoSet and Contract-NLI datasets using Gemma-3 4B, PLD improved Macro F1 scores from 57\% to 90.0\% and 67\% to 83\% respectively, enabling this compact model to match frontier performance with negligible latency overhead. These expressive instructions render the decision-making process transparent, allowing for full human verification of logic, making this approach ideal for regulated industries such as law, finance, and content moderation, as well as high-volume use cases and edge devices.

AI.tldr: Prompt-Level Distillation (PLD) extracts reasoning patterns from large teacher models into structured instructions for smaller student models, achieving frontier performance with minimal latency while maintaining interpretability.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-Thought prompting is accurate but has prohibitive latency and high inference costs, while fine-tuning smaller models sacrifices interpretability and introduces significant resource overhead. There's a need for efficient, interpretable reasoning in compact models.
AI.method: PLD extracts explicit reasoning patterns from a Teacher model and organizes them into a structured list of expressive instructions for the Student model's System Prompt, enabling transparent decision-making.
AI.result: On StereoSet and Contract-NLI datasets using Gemma-3 4B, PLD improved Macro F1 scores from 57% to 90.0% and 67% to 83% respectively, enabling compact models to match frontier performance with negligible latency overhead.
AI.conclusion: PLD provides an efficient, interpretable alternative to Chain-of-Thought prompting and fine-tuning, making it ideal for regulated industries (law, finance, content moderation), high-volume use cases, and edge devices by enabling full human verification of logic.

title: Pipeline for Verifying LLM-Generated Mathematical Solutions
summary: With the growing popularity of Large Reasoning Models and their results in solving mathematical problems, it becomes crucial to measure their capabilities. We introduce a pipeline for both automatic and interactive verification as a more accurate alternative to only checking the answer which is currently the most popular approach for benchmarks. The pipeline can also be used as a generator of correct solutions both in formal and informal languages. 3 AI agents, which can be chosen for the benchmark accordingly, are included in the structure. The key idea is the use of prompts to obtain the solution in the specific form which allows for easier verification using proof assistants and possible use of small models ($\le 8B$). Experiments on several datasets suggest low probability of False Positives. The open-source implementation with instructions on setting up a server is available at https://github.com/LogicEnj/lean4_verification_pipeline.

AI.tldr: A pipeline for automatic and interactive verification of mathematical reasoning by Large Language Models, using proof assistants and small models for verification, with open-source implementation.
AI.motivation: As Large Reasoning Models become more popular for solving mathematical problems, there's a need for more accurate evaluation methods beyond just checking final answers, which is the current standard in benchmarks.
AI.method: Introduces a pipeline with automatic and interactive verification using prompts to obtain solutions in specific formats that enable easier verification with proof assistants and small models (≤8B parameters). Includes 3 AI agents that can be selected for benchmarking.
AI.result: Experiments on several datasets show low probability of False Positives. The pipeline can also generate correct solutions in both formal and informal languages.
AI.conclusion: The proposed verification pipeline provides a more accurate alternative to answer-only checking for evaluating mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs, with open-source implementation available.

title: PVminer: A Domain-Specific Tool to Detect the Patient Voice in Patient Generated Data
summary: Patient-generated text such as secure messages, surveys, and interviews contains rich expressions of the patient voice (PV), reflecting communicative behaviors and social determinants of health (SDoH). Traditional qualitative coding frameworks are labor intensive and do not scale to large volumes of patient-authored messages across health systems. Existing machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) approaches provide partial solutions but often treat patient-centered communication (PCC) and SDoH as separate tasks or rely on models not well suited to patient-facing language. We introduce PVminer, a domain-adapted NLP framework for structuring patient voice in secure patient-provider communication. PVminer formulates PV detection as a multi-label, multi-class prediction task integrating patient-specific BERT encoders (PV-BERT-base and PV-BERT-large), unsupervised topic modeling for thematic augmentation (PV-Topic-BERT), and fine-tuned classifiers for Code, Subcode, and Combo-level labels. Topic representations are incorporated during fine-tuning and inference to enrich semantic inputs. PVminer achieves strong performance across hierarchical tasks and outperforms biomedical and clinical pre-trained baselines, achieving F1 scores of 82.25% (Code), 80.14% (Subcode), and up to 77.87% (Combo). An ablation study further shows that author identity and topic-based augmentation each contribute meaningful gains. Pre-trained models, source code, and documentation will be publicly released, with annotated datasets available upon request for research use.

AI.tldr: PVminer is a domain-adapted NLP framework that uses patient-specific BERT models and topic modeling to automatically detect patient voice (including communication behaviors and social determinants of health) in patient-generated text, outperforming existing biomedical and clinical models.
AI.motivation: Traditional qualitative coding of patient-generated text is labor-intensive and doesn't scale. Existing ML/NLP approaches either treat patient-centered communication and social determinants of health as separate tasks or use models not well-suited for patient-facing language, creating a need for a specialized framework.
AI.method: PVminer formulates patient voice detection as multi-label, multi-class prediction using patient-specific BERT encoders (PV-BERT-base/large), unsupervised topic modeling for thematic augmentation (PV-Topic-BERT), and fine-tuned classifiers for hierarchical Code, Subcode, and Combo-level labels. Topic representations are incorporated during fine-tuning and inference to enrich semantic inputs.
AI.result: PVminer achieves F1 scores of 82.25% (Code level), 80.14% (Subcode level), and up to 77.87% (Combo level), outperforming biomedical and clinical pre-trained baselines. Ablation studies show that both author identity and topic-based augmentation contribute meaningful performance gains.
AI.conclusion: PVminer provides an effective, scalable solution for automatically structuring patient voice in healthcare communications, with plans to publicly release pre-trained models, source code, documentation, and annotated datasets for research use.

title: POMDPPlanners: Open-Source Package for POMDP Planning
summary: We present POMDPPlanners, an open-source Python package for empirical evaluation of Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) planning algorithms. The package integrates state-of-the-art planning algorithms, a suite of benchmark environments with safety-critical variants, automated hyperparameter optimization via Optuna, persistent caching with failure recovery, and configurable parallel simulation -- reducing the overhead of extensive simulation studies. POMDPPlanners is designed to enable scalable, reproducible research on decision-making under uncertainty, with particular emphasis on risk-sensitive settings where standard toolkits fall short.

AI.tldr: POMDPPlanners is an open-source Python package for evaluating POMDP planning algorithms with integrated algorithms, benchmark environments, hyperparameter optimization, caching, and parallel simulation.
AI.motivation: Standard toolkits fall short for risk-sensitive POMDP research, and there's a need for scalable, reproducible evaluation of decision-making under uncertainty with reduced simulation overhead.
AI.method: Developed an integrated Python package with state-of-the-art planning algorithms, benchmark environments (including safety-critical variants), automated hyperparameter optimization via Optuna, persistent caching with failure recovery, and configurable parallel simulation.
AI.result: Created POMDPPlanners package that reduces overhead of extensive simulation studies and enables scalable, reproducible research on decision-making under uncertainty, particularly for risk-sensitive settings.
AI.conclusion: POMDPPlanners provides a comprehensive toolkit for empirical evaluation of POMDP planning algorithms, addressing limitations of existing tools and facilitating research in decision-making under uncertainty, especially in safety-critical applications.

title: On Data Engineering for Scaling LLM Terminal Capabilities
summary: Despite rapid recent progress in the terminal capabilities of large language models, the training data strategies behind state-of-the-art terminal agents remain largely undisclosed. We address this gap through a systematic study of data engineering practices for terminal agents, making two key contributions: (1) Terminal-Task-Gen, a lightweight synthetic task generation pipeline that supports seed-based and skill-based task construction, and (2) a comprehensive analysis of data and training strategies, including filtering, curriculum learning, long context training, and scaling behavior. Our pipeline yields Terminal-Corpus, a large-scale open-source dataset for terminal tasks. Using this dataset, we train Nemotron-Terminal, a family of models initialized from Qwen3(8B, 14B, 32B) that achieve substantial gains on Terminal-Bench 2.0: Nemotron-Terminal-8B improves from 2.5% to 13.0% Nemotron-Terminal-14B improves from 4.0% to 20.2%, and Nemotron-Terminal-32B improves from 3.4% to 27.4%, matching the performance of significantly larger models. To accelerate research in this domain, we open-source our model checkpoints and most of our synthetic datasets at https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nemotron-terminal.

AI.tldr: Systematic study of data engineering for terminal agents introduces Terminal-Task-Gen pipeline and Terminal-Corpus dataset, training Nemotron-Terminal models that achieve substantial performance gains on Terminal-Bench 2.0.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid progress in terminal capabilities of large language models, training data strategies for state-of-the-art terminal agents remain largely undisclosed, creating a gap in understanding effective data engineering practices for this domain.
AI.method: Developed Terminal-Task-Gen, a lightweight synthetic task generation pipeline supporting seed-based and skill-based task construction. Created Terminal-Corpus dataset using this pipeline and analyzed data/training strategies including filtering, curriculum learning, long context training, and scaling behavior. Trained Nemotron-Terminal family of models initialized from Qwen3 (8B, 14B, 32B) architectures.
AI.result: Nemotron-Terminal models achieved substantial gains on Terminal-Bench 2.0: 8B model improved from 2.5% to 13.0%, 14B model from 4.0% to 20.2%, and 32B model from 3.4% to 27.4%, matching performance of significantly larger models. All resources are open-sourced.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that systematic data engineering practices, including synthetic task generation and comprehensive training strategies, can significantly improve terminal agent performance. The open-sourcing of datasets, models, and methodology aims to accelerate research in terminal agent development.

title: Qwen-BIM: developing large language model for BIM-based design with domain-specific benchmark and dataset
summary: As the construction industry advances toward digital transformation, BIM (Building Information Modeling)-based design has become a key driver supporting intelligent construction. Despite Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential in promoting BIM-based design, the lack of specific datasets and LLM evaluation benchmarks has significantly hindered the performance of LLMs. Therefore, this paper addresses this gap by proposing: 1) an evaluation benchmark for BIM-based design together with corresponding quantitative indicators to evaluate the performance of LLMs, 2) a method for generating textual data from BIM and constructing corresponding BIM-derived datasets for LLM evaluation and fine-tuning, and 3) a fine-tuning strategy to adapt LLMs for BIM-based design. Results demonstrate that the proposed domain-specific benchmark effectively and comprehensively assesses LLM capabilities, highlighting that general LLMs are still incompetent for domain-specific tasks. Meanwhile, with the proposed benchmark and datasets, Qwen-BIM is developed and achieves a 21.0% average increase in G-Eval score compared to the base LLM model. Notably, with only 14B parameters, performance of Qwen-BIM is comparable to that of general LLMs with 671B parameters for BIM-based design tasks. Overall, this study develops the first domain-specific LLM for BIM-based design by introducing a comprehensive benchmark and high-quality dataset, which provide a solid foundation for developing BIM-related LLMs in various fields.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first domain-specific LLM for BIM-based design, addressing the lack of evaluation benchmarks and datasets by proposing a comprehensive evaluation framework, data generation method, and fine-tuning strategy.
AI.motivation: The construction industry's digital transformation through BIM-based design lacks specific datasets and evaluation benchmarks for LLMs, hindering their effective application in this domain despite their potential.
AI.method: 1) Development of an evaluation benchmark with quantitative indicators for BIM-based design LLMs; 2) Method for generating textual data from BIM models and constructing BIM-derived datasets; 3) Fine-tuning strategy to adapt LLMs for BIM-based design tasks.
AI.result: The proposed benchmark effectively assesses LLM capabilities, revealing general LLMs' incompetence for domain-specific tasks. Qwen-BIM, developed using the benchmark and datasets, achieves 21.0% average G-Eval score improvement over base LLM and matches performance of general LLMs with 671B parameters using only 14B parameters.
AI.conclusion: This study establishes the first domain-specific LLM for BIM-based design through a comprehensive benchmark and high-quality dataset, providing foundational infrastructure for developing BIM-related LLMs across various construction and design fields.

title: Pressure Reveals Character: Behavioural Alignment Evaluation at Depth
summary: Evaluating alignment in language models requires testing how they behave under realistic pressure, not just what they claim they would do. While alignment failures increasingly cause real-world harm, comprehensive evaluation frameworks with realistic multi-turn scenarios remain lacking. We introduce an alignment benchmark spanning 904 scenarios across six categories -- Honesty, Safety, Non-Manipulation, Robustness, Corrigibility, and Scheming -- validated as realistic by human raters. Our scenarios place models under conflicting instructions, simulated tool access, and multi-turn escalation to reveal behavioural tendencies that single-turn evaluations miss. Evaluating 24 frontier models using LLM judges validated against human annotations, we find that even top-performing models exhibit gaps in specific categories, while the majority of models show consistent weaknesses across the board. Factor analysis reveals that alignment behaves as a unified construct (analogous to the g-factor in cognitive research) with models scoring high on one category tending to score high on others. We publicly release the benchmark and an interactive leaderboard to support ongoing evaluation, with plans to expand scenarios in areas where we observe persistent weaknesses and to add new models as they are released.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a comprehensive alignment benchmark with 904 realistic multi-turn scenarios across six categories to evaluate language model behavior under pressure, revealing consistent weaknesses and showing alignment functions as a unified construct.
AI.motivation: Current alignment evaluations lack realistic multi-turn scenarios that test how models actually behave under pressure, not just what they claim they would do. Alignment failures are causing increasing real-world harm, necessitating more comprehensive evaluation frameworks.
AI.method: Created a benchmark with 904 scenarios across six alignment categories (Honesty, Safety, Non-Manipulation, Robustness, Corrigibility, Scheming), validated by human raters as realistic. Scenarios include conflicting instructions, simulated tool access, and multi-turn escalation. Evaluated 24 frontier models using LLM judges validated against human annotations.
AI.result: Even top-performing models show gaps in specific categories, while most models exhibit consistent weaknesses across the board. Factor analysis reveals alignment behaves as a unified construct (similar to g-factor in cognitive research), with models scoring high in one category tending to score high in others.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals significant alignment weaknesses in current models and demonstrates that alignment functions as a unified construct. The authors publicly release the benchmark and interactive leaderboard for ongoing evaluation, with plans to expand scenarios in areas of persistent weakness and add new models.

title: Diagnosing Causal Reasoning in Vision-Language Models via Structured Relevance Graphs
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) achieve strong performance on visual question answering benchmarks, yet often rely on spurious correlations rather than genuine causal reasoning. Existing evaluations primarily assess the correctness of the answers, making it unclear whether failures arise from limited reasoning capability or from misidentifying causally relevant information. We introduce Vision-Language Causal Graphs (VLCGs), a structured, query-conditioned representation that explicitly encodes causally relevant objects, attributes, relations, and scene-grounded assumptions. Building on this representation, we present ViLCaR, a diagnostic benchmark comprising tasks for Causal Attribution, Causal Inference, and Question Answering, along with graph-aligned evaluation metrics that assess relevance identification beyond final answer accuracy. Experiments in state-of-the-art LVLMs show that injecting structured relevance information significantly improves attribution and inference consistency compared to zero-shot and standard in-context learning. These findings suggest that current limitations in LVLM causal reasoning stem primarily from insufficient structural guidance rather than a lack of reasoning capacity.

AI.tldr: ViLCaR is a diagnostic benchmark that uses structured Vision-Language Causal Graphs (VLCGs) to evaluate causal reasoning in LVLMs, showing that current limitations stem from insufficient structural guidance rather than lack of reasoning capacity.
AI.motivation: Current LVLMs often rely on spurious correlations rather than genuine causal reasoning, and existing evaluations focus only on answer correctness without diagnosing whether failures come from limited reasoning capability or misidentification of causally relevant information.
AI.method: Introduces Vision-Language Causal Graphs (VLCGs) as structured, query-conditioned representations encoding causally relevant objects, attributes, relations, and scene-grounded assumptions. Builds ViLCaR benchmark with tasks for Causal Attribution, Causal Inference, and Question Answering, using graph-aligned evaluation metrics.
AI.result: Experiments show that injecting structured relevance information significantly improves attribution and inference consistency in state-of-the-art LVLMs compared to zero-shot and standard in-context learning approaches.
AI.conclusion: Current limitations in LVLM causal reasoning stem primarily from insufficient structural guidance rather than a lack of reasoning capacity, suggesting that structured representations like VLCGs can significantly enhance causal reasoning performance.

title: Predicting Sentence Acceptability Judgments in Multimodal Contexts
summary: Previous work has examined the capacity of deep neural networks (DNNs), particularly transformers, to predict human sentence acceptability judgments, both independently of context, and in document contexts. We consider the effect of prior exposure to visual images (i.e., visual context) on these judgments for humans and large language models (LLMs). Our results suggest that, in contrast to textual context, visual images appear to have little if any impact on human acceptability ratings. However, LLMs display the compression effect seen in previous work on human judgments in document contexts. Different sorts of LLMs are able to predict human acceptability judgments to a high degree of accuracy, but in general, their performance is slightly better when visual contexts are removed. Moreover, the distribution of LLM judgments varies among models, with Qwen resembling human patterns, and others diverging from them. LLM-generated predictions on sentence acceptability are highly correlated with their normalised log probabilities in general. However, the correlations decrease when visual contexts are present, suggesting that a higher gap exists between the internal representations of LLMs and their generated predictions in the presence of visual contexts. Our experimental work suggests interesting points of similarity and of difference between human and LLM processing of sentences in multimodal contexts.

AI.tldr: Visual context has minimal impact on human sentence acceptability judgments but affects LLMs differently, with performance slightly better without visual context and varying patterns across models.
AI.motivation: To investigate how visual context (prior exposure to images) affects sentence acceptability judgments in humans versus large language models, contrasting with previous work on textual/document contexts.
AI.method: Examined human and LLM sentence acceptability judgments with and without visual context, comparing different LLM types, analyzing correlations with normalized log probabilities, and assessing compression effects.
AI.result: Visual context has little impact on human ratings but affects LLMs: performance slightly better without visual context, Qwen resembles human patterns while others diverge, correlations between LLM predictions and log probabilities decrease with visual context.
AI.conclusion: Visual context reveals interesting similarities and differences between human and LLM sentence processing: minimal human impact vs. varied LLM effects, suggesting gaps between LLM internal representations and predictions in multimodal contexts.

title: HELP: HyperNode Expansion and Logical Path-Guided Evidence Localization for Accurate and Efficient GraphRAG
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with inherent knowledge boundaries and hallucinations, limiting their reliability in knowledge-intensive tasks. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates these issues, it frequently overlooks structural interdependencies essential for multi-hop reasoning. Graph-based RAG approaches attempt to bridge this gap, yet they typically face trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency due to challenges such as costly graph traversals and semantic noise in LLM-generated summaries. In this paper, we propose HyperNode Expansion and Logical Path-Guided Evidence Localization strategies for GraphRAG (HELP), a novel framework designed to balance accuracy with practical efficiency through two core strategies: 1) HyperNode Expansion, which iteratively chains knowledge triplets into coherent reasoning paths abstracted as HyperNodes to capture complex structural dependencies and ensure retrieval accuracy; and 2) Logical Path-Guided Evidence Localization, which leverages precomputed graph-text correlations to map these paths directly to the corpus for superior efficiency. HELP avoids expensive random walks and semantic distortion, preserving knowledge integrity while drastically reducing retrieval latency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HELP achieves competitive performance across multiple simple and multi-hop QA benchmarks and up to a 28.8$\times$ speedup over leading Graph-based RAG baselines.

AI.tldr: HELP is a GraphRAG framework that balances accuracy and efficiency through HyperNode Expansion for structural reasoning and Logical Path-Guided Evidence Localization for fast retrieval, achieving competitive QA performance with 28.8× speedup.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with knowledge boundaries and hallucinations in knowledge-intensive tasks. While RAG helps, it overlooks structural interdependencies needed for multi-hop reasoning. Graph-based RAG approaches exist but face accuracy-efficiency trade-offs due to costly graph traversals and semantic noise in LLM-generated summaries.
AI.method: HELP uses two core strategies: 1) HyperNode Expansion - iteratively chains knowledge triplets into coherent reasoning paths abstracted as HyperNodes to capture complex structural dependencies; 2) Logical Path-Guided Evidence Localization - leverages precomputed graph-text correlations to map these paths directly to the corpus for efficiency, avoiding expensive random walks and semantic distortion.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show HELP achieves competitive performance across multiple simple and multi-hop QA benchmarks and achieves up to 28.8× speedup over leading Graph-based RAG baselines.
AI.conclusion: HELP effectively balances accuracy with practical efficiency in GraphRAG by preserving knowledge integrity while drastically reducing retrieval latency, addressing key limitations of existing approaches through its novel strategies.

title: Architecting AgentOS: From Token-Level Context to Emergent System-Level Intelligence
summary: The paradigm of Large Language Models is undergoing a fundamental transition from static inference engines to dynamic autonomous cognitive systems.While current research primarily focuses on scaling context windows or optimizing prompt engineering the theoretical bridge between micro scale token processing and macro scale systemic intelligence remains fragmented.This paper proposes AgentOS,a holistic conceptual framework that redefines the LLM as a "Reasoning Kernel" governed by structured operating system logic.Central to this architecture is Deep Context Management which conceptualizes the context window as an Addressable Semantic Space rather than a passive buffer.We systematically deconstruct the transition from discrete sequences to coherent cognitive states introducing mechanisms for Semantic Slicing and Temporal Alignment to mitigate cognitive drift in multi-agent orchestration.By mapping classical OS abstractions such as memory paging interrupt handling and process scheduling onto LLM native constructs, this review provides a rigorous roadmap for architecting resilient scalable and self-evolving cognitive environments.Our analysis asserts that the next frontier of AGI development lies in the architectural efficiency of system-level coordination.

AI.tldr: AgentOS proposes a conceptual framework that redefines LLMs as "Reasoning Kernels" with operating system-like architecture, introducing Deep Context Management to treat context windows as Addressable Semantic Spaces for better cognitive state coherence.
AI.motivation: Current LLM research focuses on scaling context windows and prompt engineering, but lacks theoretical bridge between micro-scale token processing and macro-scale systemic intelligence. There's a need for architectural frameworks that enable resilient, scalable, and self-evolving cognitive environments.
AI.method: Proposes AgentOS framework with Deep Context Management that conceptualizes context window as Addressable Semantic Space. Introduces Semantic Slicing and Temporal Alignment mechanisms to mitigate cognitive drift. Maps classical OS abstractions (memory paging, interrupt handling, process scheduling) onto LLM native constructs.
AI.result: Provides a rigorous roadmap for architecting resilient, scalable, and self-evolving cognitive environments. The framework enables systematic deconstruction of transition from discrete sequences to coherent cognitive states in multi-agent orchestration.
AI.conclusion: The next frontier of AGI development lies in architectural efficiency of system-level coordination. AgentOS offers a holistic conceptual framework for transitioning LLMs from static inference engines to dynamic autonomous cognitive systems through structured operating system logic.

title: A Benchmark for Deep Information Synthesis
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly used to solve complex tasks involving tool use, such as web browsing, code execution, and data analysis. However, current evaluation benchmarks do not adequately assess their ability to solve real-world tasks that require synthesizing information from multiple sources and inferring insights beyond simple fact retrieval. To address this, we introduce DEEPSYNTH, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate agents on realistic, time-consuming problems that combine information gathering, synthesis, and structured reasoning to produce insights. DEEPSYNTH contains 120 tasks collected across 7 domains and data sources covering 67 countries. DEEPSYNTH is constructed using a multi-stage data collection pipeline that requires annotators to collect official data sources, create hypotheses, perform manual analysis, and design tasks with verifiable answers. When evaluated on DEEPSYNTH, 11 state-of-the-art LLMs and deep research agents achieve a maximum F1 score of 8.97 and 17.5 on the LLM-judge metric, underscoring the difficulty of the benchmark. Our analysis reveals that current agents struggle with hallucinations and reasoning over large information spaces, highlighting DEEPSYNTH as a crucial benchmark for guiding future research.

AI.tldr: DEEPSYNTH is a new benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents on realistic, complex tasks requiring information synthesis and reasoning across multiple sources, showing current models perform poorly (max F1 8.97-17.5).
AI.motivation: Current evaluation benchmarks fail to adequately assess LLM-based agents' ability to solve real-world tasks that require synthesizing information from multiple sources and inferring insights beyond simple fact retrieval.
AI.method: Created DEEPSYNTH benchmark with 120 tasks across 7 domains and 67 countries using a multi-stage data collection pipeline where annotators collect official data sources, create hypotheses, perform manual analysis, and design tasks with verifiable answers.
AI.result: When evaluated on DEEPSYNTH, 11 state-of-the-art LLMs and deep research agents achieve a maximum F1 score of 8.97 and 17.5 on the LLM-judge metric, demonstrating the benchmark's difficulty.
AI.conclusion: Current agents struggle with hallucinations and reasoning over large information spaces, highlighting DEEPSYNTH as a crucial benchmark for guiding future research in LLM-based agent development.

title: LogicGraph : Benchmarking Multi-Path Logical Reasoning via Neuro-Symbolic Generation and Verification
summary: Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) primarily emphasize convergent logical reasoning, where success is defined by producing a single correct proof. However, many real-world reasoning problems admit multiple valid derivations, requiring models to explore diverse logical paths rather than committing to one route. To address this limitation, we introduce LogicGraph, the first benchmark aimed to systematically evaluate multi-path logical reasoning, constructed via a neuro-symbolic framework that leverages backward logic generation and semantic instantiation. This pipeline yields solver-verified reasoning problems formalized by high-depth multi-path reasoning and inherent logical distractions, where each instance is associated with an exhaustive set of minimal proofs. We further propose a reference-free evaluation framework to rigorously assess model performance in both convergent and divergent regimes. Experiments on state-of-the-art language models reveal a common limitation: models tend to commit early to a single route and fail to explore alternatives, and the coverage gap grows substantially with reasoning depth. LogicGraph exposes this divergence gap and provides actionable insights to motivate future improvements. Our code and data will be released at https://github.com/kkkkarry/LogicGraph.

AI.tldr: LogicGraph is a benchmark for evaluating multi-path logical reasoning in LLMs, revealing models' tendency to commit early to single solutions rather than exploring diverse valid derivations.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluations focus on convergent reasoning (single correct proof), but real-world problems often have multiple valid derivations requiring exploration of diverse logical paths.
AI.method: Neuro-symbolic framework using backward logic generation and semantic instantiation to create solver-verified reasoning problems with high-depth multi-path reasoning and logical distractions, each with exhaustive minimal proofs.
AI.result: State-of-the-art LLMs show common limitation: early commitment to single routes, failure to explore alternatives, with coverage gap growing substantially with reasoning depth.
AI.conclusion: LogicGraph exposes the divergence gap in LLM reasoning and provides actionable insights for future improvements in multi-path logical reasoning capabilities.

title: Aletheia tackles FirstProof autonomously
summary: We report the performance of Aletheia (Feng et al., 2026b), a mathematics research agent powered by Gemini 3 Deep Think, on the inaugural FirstProof challenge. Within the allowed timeframe of the challenge, Aletheia autonomously solved 6 problems (2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10) out of 10 according to majority expert assessments; we note that experts were not unanimous on Problem 8 (only). For full transparency, we explain our interpretation of FirstProof and disclose details about our experiments as well as our evaluation. Raw prompts and outputs are available at https://github.com/google-deepmind/superhuman/tree/main/aletheia.

AI.tldr: Aletheia, a mathematics research agent using Gemini 3 Deep Think, solved 6 out of 10 problems in the FirstProof challenge within the allowed timeframe, with expert consensus on all but one problem.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the capabilities of autonomous mathematics research agents by participating in the inaugural FirstProof challenge and evaluating performance against expert human standards.
AI.method: Used Aletheia, a mathematics research agent powered by Gemini 3 Deep Think, to autonomously solve problems within the FirstProof challenge timeframe. Employed expert assessment for evaluation with full transparency about interpretation and experimental details.
AI.result: Aletheia solved 6 out of 10 problems (specifically problems 2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10) according to majority expert assessments. Experts were not unanimous only on Problem 8. All raw prompts and outputs are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: The Aletheia mathematics research agent demonstrated significant capability in autonomous mathematical problem-solving, successfully solving the majority of FirstProof challenge problems, though expert disagreement on one problem highlights remaining challenges in evaluation.

title: Tool Building as a Path to "Superintelligence"
summary: The Diligent Learner framework suggests LLMs can achieve superintelligence via test-time search, provided a sufficient step-success probability $γ$. In this work, we design a benchmark to measure $γ$ on logical out-of-distribution inference. We construct a class of tasks involving GF(2) circuit reconstruction that grow more difficult with each reasoning step, and that are, from an information-theoretic standpoint, impossible to reliably solve unless the LLM carefully integrates all of the information provided. Our analysis demonstrates that while the $γ$ value for small LLMs declines superlinearly as depth increases, frontier models exhibit partial robustness on this task. Furthermore, we find that successful reasoning at scale is contingent upon precise tool calls, identifying tool design as a critical capability for LLMs to achieve general superintelligence through the Diligent Learner framework.

AI.tldr: LLMs' ability to achieve superintelligence via test-time search depends on step-success probability γ, measured on logical OOD inference tasks involving GF(2) circuit reconstruction that become progressively harder with each step.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether LLMs can achieve superintelligence through the Diligent Learner framework, which requires maintaining sufficient step-success probability (γ) during test-time search, particularly on challenging logical out-of-distribution inference tasks.
AI.method: Designed a benchmark to measure γ on logical OOD inference by constructing tasks involving GF(2) circuit reconstruction that grow more difficult with each reasoning step and require careful integration of all provided information to solve reliably.
AI.result: Small LLMs show superlinear decline in γ as depth increases, while frontier models exhibit partial robustness. Successful reasoning at scale depends on precise tool calls, identifying tool design as critical for achieving general superintelligence.
AI.conclusion: Tool design is a critical capability for LLMs to achieve general superintelligence through the Diligent Learner framework, as precise tool calls enable successful reasoning at scale on challenging logical inference tasks.

title: Motivation is Something You Need
summary: This work introduces a novel training paradigm that draws from affective neuroscience. Inspired by the interplay of emotions and cognition in the human brain and more specifically the SEEKING motivational state, we design a dual-model framework where a smaller base model is trained continuously, while a larger motivated model is activated intermittently during predefined "motivation conditions". The framework mimics the emotional state of high curiosity and anticipation of reward in which broader brain regions are recruited to enhance cognitive performance. Exploiting scalable architectures where larger models extend smaller ones, our method enables shared weight updates and selective expansion of network capacity during noteworthy training steps. Empirical evaluation on the image classification task demonstrates that, not only does the alternating training scheme efficiently and effectively enhance the base model compared to a traditional scheme, in some cases, the motivational model also surpasses its standalone counterpart despite seeing less data per epoch. This opens the possibility of simultaneously training two models tailored to different deployment constraints with competitive or superior performance while keeping training cost lower than when training the larger model.

AI.motivation: Inspired by affective neuroscience and the interplay between emotions and cognition in the human brain, particularly the SEEKING motivational state where curiosity and reward anticipation recruit broader brain regions to enhance cognitive performance. title: The Initial Exploration Problem in Knowledge Graph Exploration
summary: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) enable the integration and representation of complex information across domains, but their semantic richness and structural complexity create substantial barriers for lay users without expertise in semantic web technologies. When encountering an unfamiliar KG, such users face a distinct orientation challenge: they do not know what questions are possible, how the knowledge is structured, or how to begin exploration. This paper identifies and theorises this phenomenon as the Initial Exploration Problem (IEP). Drawing on theories from information behaviour and human-computer interaction, including ASK, exploratory search, information foraging, and cognitive load theory, we develop a conceptual framing of the IEP characterised by three interdependent barriers: scope uncertainty, ontology opacity, and query incapacity. We argue that these barriers converge at the moment of first contact, distinguishing the IEP from related concepts that presuppose an existing starting point or information goal. Analysing KG exploration interfaces at the level of interaction primitives, we suggest that many systems rely on epistemic assumptions that do not hold at first contact. This reveals a structural gap in the design space: the absence of interaction primitives for scope revelation, mechanisms that communicate what a KG contains without requiring users to formulate queries or interpret ontological structures. In articulating the IEP, this paper provides a theoretical lens for evaluating KG interfaces and for designing entry-point scaffolding that supports initial exploration.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies the Initial Exploration Problem (IEP) in Knowledge Graphs - the challenge lay users face when first encountering an unfamiliar KG due to scope uncertainty, ontology opacity, and query incapacity, and proposes theoretical framing and design implications.
AI.motivation: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are semantically rich and structurally complex, creating substantial barriers for lay users without semantic web expertise. These users face an orientation challenge when encountering unfamiliar KGs: they don't know what questions are possible, how knowledge is structured, or how to begin exploration.
AI.method: The paper draws on theories from information behaviour and human-computer interaction (ASK, exploratory search, information foraging, cognitive load theory) to develop a conceptual framing of the IEP. It analyzes KG exploration interfaces at the level of interaction primitives and identifies structural gaps in design.
AI.result: The paper identifies three interdependent barriers characterizing the IEP: scope uncertainty (not knowing what the KG contains), ontology opacity (not understanding the structure), and query incapacity (not knowing how to formulate queries). It reveals a structural gap in KG interface design: the absence of interaction primitives for scope revelation that communicate KG content without requiring query formulation or ontology interpretation.
AI.conclusion: By articulating the Initial Exploration Problem, the paper provides a theoretical lens for evaluating KG interfaces and designing entry-point scaffolding that supports initial exploration. It distinguishes IEP from related concepts by focusing on the moment of first contact before users have starting points or information goals.

title: CG-DMER: Hybrid Contrastive-Generative Framework for Disentangled Multimodal ECG Representation Learning
summary: Accurate interpretation of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals is crucial for diagnosing cardiovascular diseases. Recent multimodal approaches that integrate ECGs with accompanying clinical reports show strong potential, but they still face two main concerns from a modality perspective: (1) intra-modality: existing models process ECGs in a lead-agnostic manner, overlooking spatial-temporal dependencies across leads, which restricts their effectiveness in modeling fine-grained diagnostic patterns; (2) inter-modality: existing methods directly align ECG signals with clinical reports, introducing modality-specific biases due to the free-text nature of the reports. In light of these two issues, we propose CG-DMER, a contrastive-generative framework for disentangled multimodal ECG representation learning, powered by two key designs: (1) Spatial-temporal masked modeling is designed to better capture fine-grained temporal dynamics and inter-lead spatial dependencies by applying masking across both spatial and temporal dimensions and reconstructing the missing information. (2) A representation disentanglement and alignment strategy is designed to mitigate unnecessary noise and modality-specific biases by introducing modality-specific and modality-shared encoders, ensuring a clearer separation between modality-invariant and modality-specific representations. Experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that CG-DMER achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: CG-DMER is a contrastive-generative framework for multimodal ECG representation learning that addresses lead-agnostic processing and modality-specific biases through spatial-temporal masked modeling and representation disentanglement.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal ECG approaches have two main limitations: (1) intra-modality - lead-agnostic processing overlooks spatial-temporal dependencies across ECG leads, limiting fine-grained pattern modeling; (2) inter-modality - direct alignment of ECG signals with free-text clinical reports introduces modality-specific biases.
AI.method: Proposes CG-DMER with two key designs: (1) Spatial-temporal masked modeling applies masking across both spatial (leads) and temporal dimensions and reconstructs missing information to capture fine-grained temporal dynamics and inter-lead spatial dependencies. (2) Representation disentanglement and alignment uses modality-specific and modality-shared encoders to separate modality-invariant from modality-specific representations, mitigating noise and biases.
AI.result: Experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that CG-DMER achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: CG-DMER effectively addresses both intra-modality and inter-modality challenges in multimodal ECG analysis through spatial-temporal masked modeling and representation disentanglement, leading to superior performance on various downstream tasks.

title: NoRD: A Data-Efficient Vision-Language-Action Model that Drives without Reasoning
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are advancing autonomous driving by replacing modular pipelines with unified end-to-end architectures. However, current VLAs face two expensive requirements: (1) massive dataset collection, and (2) dense reasoning annotations. In this work, we address both challenges with \modelname (\textbf{No} \textbf{R}easoning for \textbf{D}riving). Compared to existing VLAs, \modelname achieves competitive performance while being fine-tuned on $<$60\% of the data and no reasoning annotations, resulting in 3$\times$ fewer tokens. We identify that standard Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) fails to yield significant improvements when applied to policies trained on such small, reasoning-free datasets. We show that this limitation stems from difficulty bias, which disproportionately penalizes reward signals from scenarios that produce high-variance rollouts within GRPO. \modelname overcomes this by incorporating Dr.~GRPO, a recent algorithm designed to mitigate difficulty bias in LLMs. As a result, \modelname achieves competitive performance on Waymo and NAVSIM with a fraction of the training data and no reasoning overhead, enabling more efficient autonomous systems.

AI.tldr: NoRD is a Vision-Language-Action model for autonomous driving that achieves competitive performance using <60% of training data and no reasoning annotations, reducing tokens by 3× through Dr. GRPO optimization to overcome difficulty bias.
AI.motivation: Current Vision-Language-Action models for autonomous driving require massive dataset collection and dense reasoning annotations, which are expensive and resource-intensive to obtain.
AI.method: NoRD uses Dr. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) algorithm to mitigate difficulty bias that arises when training on small, reasoning-free datasets, enabling effective policy optimization without reasoning annotations.
AI.result: NoRD achieves competitive performance on Waymo and NAVSIM benchmarks while being fine-tuned on <60% of the data and no reasoning annotations, resulting in 3× fewer tokens compared to existing VLAs.
AI.conclusion: NoRD enables more efficient autonomous driving systems by reducing data requirements and eliminating the need for expensive reasoning annotations while maintaining competitive performance.
